These concentrations are low and are not believed to be indicative of water quality problems. Cooper, chromium, maganese, mercury, and nickel concentrations in the sediments of the reservoir were below those levels reported for natural soils. Arsenic, cadmium, lead, silver, and zinc were above the level reported for natural soils. However, comparable levels have been found in many other Texas reservoirs (except silver). Since no areas of gross accumulations were found, and the concentrations indicate no geographical trends, the heavy metals concentrations in Amistad Reservoir are considered natural and not indicative of water quality problems (TWQB, undated).
2.28 Even though stratification generally occurs in winter and summer months, it is not likely to be significant at Amistad during winter months as evidenced by thermal studies conducted from October 1968 to January 1973 by the US Department of the Interior, Geological Survey. Unfortunately, there are no dissolved cyygen data for this period to support these findings. Stratification does occur in Amistad Reservoir during late summer and early fall which results in marked depression of dissolved oxygen (EPA, 1976). In addition, near zero or zero oxygen levels can cause increases in ammonia, phosphates, and sulfides near the bottom of the reservoir. Data available for Amistad Reservoir indicate only slight increases in ammonia-nitrogen and dissolved ortho-phosphates with depth during October 1974, at which time the overall dissolved oxygen levels were the lowest occurring in the available data. Oxygen levels during August were also depressed, but corresponding data covering other parameters are not available. Data for March and May revealed that oxygen was not a problem in the lower end of the reservoir.
2.29 Ground Water. Storage in Amistad Reservoir has caused a rise in the ground water table adjacent to the reservoir. Although some of the water in side storage is from Amistad Reservoir, most is ground water which formerly moved toward and discharged to Rio Grande. This side storage responds to changes in the level of Amistad Reservoir, although drainage of the formation will extend over many months should a prolonged drought result in a major drawdown of Amistad Reservoir.
2.30 Amistad Fishery. The Amistad fishery is generally characteristic of other West Texas lakes in having a larger percentage of nongame over game species. The primary game fishes native to the reservoir are largemouth bass, channel catfish, flathead catfish, Rio Grande blue catfish, white bass, bluegill, and white crappie. The two predominant nongame species are smallmouth buffalo and gizzard shad, with river carpsucker, carp, and gar also prevalent. Recent surveys by TPWD indicate 54 species of fish to be present in the reservoir (Follis, 1973). In an effort to utilize the nongame species that were not being controlled by native predators, the TPWD stocked exotic open water predator species. These stockings initiated in 1974 included striped bass, walleye, smallmouth bass, Florida largemouth bass and northern pike. Existing native populations were also supplemented by stockings. Habitat conducive to good sport fish reproduction is limited in Amistad Reservoir. The basin is typically rough, stairstep canyons of limestone and clay. The majority of the reservoir consists of deep, clear, open water.
2.31 Soils. Upland soils in the Amistad Reservoir area are classified as Aridosols, and characteristically are relatively thin, soft, unleached, with little or no change in clay content of underlying layers. Limestone bedrock or lime accumulations (caliche) are usually encountered within 20 inches of the surface.
